claims.claim: Philosophy of science is the philosophical examination of scientific practice, including its methods, concepts, aims, and assumptions; debates in the field concern the very nature of scientific knowledge.

The demarcation problem asks how to meaningfully and reliably separate science from pseudoscience, and Karl Popper's falsifiability criterion — a theory is scientific when it is incompatible with some possible observations — is the most influential modern proposal.

Popper's falsifiability faces standard problems: logically a single counter-instance falsifies a universal claim, but in practice testing involves auxiliary assumptions (the Duhem-Quine point), theories can be protected by ad hoc modification, some pseudoscientific claims are falsifiable and false, and some accepted science is at times unfalsifiable; critics include Kuhn, Lakatos, and Feyerabend, and Laudan argued the problem is insoluble while others responded with new proposals.

Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) describes mature science as normal puzzle-solving within a paradigm, with anomalies leading to crisis and revolutionary paradigm change; his claims about incommensurability are controversial.
Observation is theory-laden: what a scientist observes is shaped by the theories and expectations they already hold.

Underdetermination of scientific theory by evidence is the idea that evidence available at a given time may be insufficient to determine which theory to accept; the same data can fit multiple theories, but the claim is disputed — Laudan and Leplin argue there is no guarantee that empirically equivalent rivals exist.

Scientific realism holds that well-confirmed theories are approximately true and that the entities they postulate exist; the no-miracles argument (associated with Putnam) supports realism, while the pessimistic meta-induction — most past theories were later regarded as false, so current ones likely will be too — challenges it.
Constructive empiricism (van Fraassen) holds that science aims at empirical adequacy — truth about what is observable — rather than truth about unobservables, making it a representative antirealism.

The deductive-nomological model (Hempel and Oppenheim) treats a scientific explanation as a deduction of the phenomenon from general laws together with initial conditions; it targets explanations of why things happen rather than how-to instructions, and it faces well-known objections such as explanatory asymmetries and irrelevancies.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does falsifiability separate science from pseudoscience?
positions: Popper: a theory is scientific when it is incompatible with some possible observations; physics and chemistry qualify, while astrology and phrenology do not.

Critics (Kuhn, Lakatos, Feyerabend; later Laudan's 1983 'demise' paper): the criterion fails in practice because testing involves auxiliary assumptions, theories can be protected by ad hoc adjustment, and some pseudoscientific claims are falsifiable while some accepted science is not; Laudan declared the problem insoluble, and others responded with new demarcation proposals.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents falsifiability as an influential proposal and attributes the criticisms and the ongoing debate without adjudicating.

positions: Duhem and Quine: a failed prediction tests a whole web of assumptions, and evidence alone cannot force a unique theory; theoretical virtues such as simplicity and conservatism guide choice.
Laudan and Leplin: there is no guarantee that empirically equivalent rivals exist, so underdetermination need not follow from any given body of evidence.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents underdetermination as a real but contested challenge with limits, and explicitly avoids the overreach that all theories are equally good.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do theories describe an unobservable reality?
positions: Scientific realism: well-confirmed theories are approximately true and their entities exist; the no-miracles argument says realism best explains the striking success of science.

Antirealism (e.g., constructive empiricism): science aims at empirical adequacy, and the pessimistic meta-induction argues that past successful theories were later abandoned, so current theories likely will be too.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both sides neutrally with the standard arguments and responses, attributing each move to its proponents.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does paradigm change make science irrational or non-cumulative?
positions: Kuhn: revolutionary change involves incommensurability, where standards and meanings do not translate cleanly across paradigms.
Critics: incommensurability is overstated, and scientific change remains rationally assessable.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes incommensurability to Kuhn and notes that it is contested, without endorsing either reading.

sourceRecords.title: Scientific Revolutions
sourceRecords.notes: Read the entry directly from plato.stanford.edu on 2026-08-21. Supports Kuhn's account: paradigms define normal science as convergent puzzle-solving; anomalies are expected and can provoke crisis; promising alternatives bring paradigm change; incommensurability is a controversial claim; theory-ladenness of observation is attributed to Hanson. Reference only; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Karl Popper
sourceRecords.notes: Read the entry directly from plato.stanford.edu on 2026-08-21. Supports: demarcation as Popper's central problem of philosophy of science; falsifiability as the criterion (incompatibility with possible empirical observations marks science, while theories compatible with all observations are unscientific); physics and chemistry classified as sciences with psychoanalysis as pre-science and astrology and phrenology as pseudo-sciences; the distinction between the logic of falsifiability and its applied methodology. Reference only; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Scientific Realism
sourceRecords.notes: Read the entry directly from plato.stanford.edu on 2026-08-21. Supports: realism as the view that best theories give true or approximately true descriptions of observable and unobservable aspects of a mind-independent world; the no-miracles argument after Putnam's claim that realism is the only philosophy that does not make the success of science a miracle; the pessimistic induction as an argument from the history of theory turnover (with Poincare and Putnam versions); van Fraassen's constructive empiricism as the view that science aims at empirical adequacy. Reference only; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Underdetermination of Scientific Theory
sourceRecords.notes: Read the entry directly from plato.stanford.edu on 2026-08-21. Supports: the core idea that evidence available at a time may be insufficient to determine what beliefs to hold; Duhem's point that a single experiment tests a hypothesis together with auxiliary assumptions (Foucault's light-in-water episode); Quine's holism and the web of belief with theoretical virtues (simplicity, conservatism, scope, fecundity); Laudan and Leplin's argument that underdetermination can be defeated because empirically equivalent rivals are not guaranteed. Reference only; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: 20th Century Theories of Scientific Explanation
sourceRecords.notes: Read on 2026-08-21 at the replacement entry URL (the former 'Scientific Explanation' entry was retired and re-published under this title, per the SEP redirect page). Supports: the deductive-nomological model as the most detailed and influential statement of scientific explanation, due to Hempel (and Hempel and Oppenheim 1948), with explanation as derivation of the explanandum from laws and initial conditions; that these models target explanations of why things happen rather than how-to explanations or meanings; well-known objections including explanatory asymmetries (flagpole and shadow) and explanatory irrelevancies (Salmon's birth-control-pills example). Reference only; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Pseudoscience and the Demarcation Problem
sourceRecords.notes: Read the article directly from iep.utm.edu on 2026-08-21. Independent Tier B cross-check for the demarcation problem: Popper as the most influential modern philosopher on demarcation; the consensus that his criterion does not work as stated; the Duhem-Quine theses and the 1919 eclipse test of general relativity; the ad hoc hypothesis problem (Le Verrier's hypotheses); that some pseudoscientific notions are falsifiable and have been shown false (astrology, Carlson 1985) while some accepted science is at times unfalsifiable (string theory); critiques by Kuhn, Lakatos, and Feyerabend and Laudan's 1983 'The Demise of the Demarcation Problem' with later responses. Reference only; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Scientific Realism and Antirealism
sourceRecords.notes: Read the article directly from iep.utm.edu on 2026-08-21. Independent Tier B cross-check for the realism debate: realism as the view that well-confirmed theories are approximately true, that the entities they postulate exist, and that we have good reason to believe their main tenets; antirealists as less optimistic; van Fraassen's characterization of realism's commitments (SR1/SR2); the no-miracles argument; Laudan's pessimistic induction as a historical challenge to realism; constructive empiricism and empirical adequacy. Reference only; no prose adapted.
